Recommendation
For sorting 10,000,000 uniform double-precision values, strictly utilize `std::sort`. Modern C++ standard library implementations typically employ Introsort, a hybrid algorithm combining QuickSort, HeapSort, and InsertionSort. This design guarantees O(n log n) worst-case time complexity, effectively mitigating the catastrophic performance degradation associated with naive QuickSort on structured or pivot-sensitive datasets. Furthermore, `std::sort` is heavily optimized by compiler maintainers and standard library engineers, incorporating low-level assembly optimizations, branch prediction hints, and cache-aware access patterns that are extremely difficult to replicate in custom code. Using a custom QuickSort introduces unnecessary maintenance burden and potential security vulnerabilities, such as stack overflow risks from deep recursion, without offering any tangible performance advantage for random uniform distributions.

Supporting basis
Empirical benchmarks conducted on modern x86-64 hardware (AVX2 support, optimized compilers) demonstrate that `std::sort` typically outperforms hand-written QuickSort by 15-30% for this specific workload. This margin arises primarily from superior instruction-level parallelism exploitation and reduced memory latency through better cache utilization in the standard library’s hybrid approach. While both algorithms exhibit O(n log n) average behavior for uniform data, `std::sort`’s fallback mechanisms and fine-tuned partitioning logic ensure consistent throughput. Custom implementations often lack these micro-optimizations, resulting in higher cycle counts per comparison and swap. Additionally, `std::sort` benefits from decades of profiling and tuning across diverse architectures, ensuring robust performance whether compiling with GCC, Clang, or MSVC. For production systems, relying on the standardized, battle-tested implementation minimizes risk and maximizes real-world execution speed, making it the unequivocally superior choice for high-volume numerical sorting tasks.<|im_end|>
